executive_assessment.text: Mykolaiv's historical water-system damage and proposed Southern Bug supply illustrate why recovery choices need scenario-specific water planning; future modeled shares include environmental flows.
Canal monitoring adds combined water-quality pressures, while municipal energy support and attack-related delays concern service resilience, not demonstrated climate-adaptation outcomes.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2024-10-02 reports: Military operations destroyed Mykolaiv’s Dnipro intake on 12 April 2022, cutting drinking water to the city’s roughly 470,000 residents.

Source dated 2024-10-02 reports: By 2024, remote-area wells yielded 5,000–10,000 m³/day against pre-war demand of at least 80,000; reported quality exceeded drinking-water limits and water was trucked daily.
For Mykolaiv's proposed Southern Bug alternative, the study models water-supply plus minimum environmental-flow requirements reaching 40–79% of flow in May–October 2051–2080 under SSP5-8.5.
Source dated 2026-04-25 reports: The study says the 2023 Kakhovka destruction increased the Dnipro–Donbas canal’s importance as a water and food-security route for Ukraine’s steppe zone.

Source dated 2026-04-25 reports: From 2015–2024, up to one-quarter of sampled canal water during low-flow periods was classed as only limited-suitability irrigation water; the authors attribute salinity changes to low flows, evaporation and combined climate and infrastructure pressures.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification. Routine/default app-use approval does not certify claims or sources. 25 of 25 evidence records and 6 of 6 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.
Ukraine lacks an integrated, current, high-resolution climate baseline that reflects war-altered land, population, infrastructure, hydrology, monitoring coverage, and occupied-territory uncertainty.

Independent response evaluation is localized to Mykolaiv; climate-integrated reconstruction, municipal adaptation, displacement integration, ecosystem recovery, and unintended distributional effects remain largely unevaluated.

The fcv-to-climate reverse pathway is well supported qualitatively through infrastructure, access, displacement, and environmental damage, but its additional effect on future climate losses and adaptation performance is not quantified.
Territorially comparable evidence disaggregated by gender, age, disability, displacement status, livelihood, and occupied or frontline location remains incomplete.
Mykolaiv's 2024 and 2025 regional climate-risk PDFs were listed by the official regional page but their substantive text was inaccessible; no findings are inferred from their metadata.
The Dnipro–Donbas paper reports sparse sampling (three campaigns per growing season), so short salinity peaks may be missed.

No inspected new source establishes a named violence-to-climate-adaptation interruption; conflict-related water and energy damage is reported separately from climate pressures except where the canal authors explicitly describe combined pressures.
Municipal solar and distributed-generation evidence is national or multi-city aggregate; named-city allocation and independent service-continuity evaluation are not provided.
Routine/default app-use approval granted by Lindsey Jones on 2026-10-27; independent source verification remains incomplete. Lending eligibility is not an FCV classification.
